summary.text: Above the thresholds, a counted representation immediately gives Goldbach for even inputs and Lemoine for odd inputs by taking \(p=n-q\) or \(p=n-2q\); explicit finite lists of prime decompositions cover all smaller admissible inputs. For any bound \(a\), applying the hypothesis to \(n=2\max(4007,a+7)\) yields \(q<n/2\), so the prime pair \((n-q-6,n-q)\) lies above \(a\), proving infinitely many cousin-prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. Define \(A(n)\) to be the number of natural numbers \(q<n\) satisfying
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,\qquad q\text{ prime},\qquad q+6\text{ prime},
\]
and
\[
 n-c(n)q\text{ prime},\qquad n-c(n)q-6\text{ prime}.
\]
If we put
\[
 p=n-c(n)q,
\]
then the inequality \((c(n)+1)q<n\) says precisely that \(p>q\), and the displayed conditions say that \(p,q,p-6,q+6\) are all prime. Hence this is exactly the sequence in the question: for even \(n\) it counts representations \(n=p+q\), while for odd \(n\) it counts representations \(n=p+2q\), in both cases with the additional four primality conditions.

Assume the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(A(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(A(n)>0\).

We prove in turn Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs.

Before doing so, we record the two bounded facts needed to bridge the thresholds in the hypothesis.

**Finite bounded facts.**

1. Every even integer \(n\) with \(4\le n\le8012\) is a sum of two primes.
2. Every odd integer \(n\) with \(7\le n\le15727\) has the form \(n=p+2q\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are prime.

Here is the precise finite computation establishing these facts. For the first fact, write \(n=2k\). The bounds on \(n\) become
\[
 2\le k\le4006.
\]
For every integer \(k\) in that interval, a pair of primes \((r,s)\) was tabulated with
\[
 2k=r+s.
\]
The tabulation was divided into the consecutive blocks
\[
[2,101], [102,201], [202,301],\ldots,[3902,4001],[4002,4006].
\]
Each line of the table consists simply of the two proposed summands; the equality with \(2k\) is an integer addition, and primality is checked by trial division through the square root. For example, the first values \(k=2,3,4,5\) use, respectively,
\[
4=2+2,\quad 6=3+3,\quad 8=3+5,\quad 10=3+7.
\]
The last five values use
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k&2k=r+s\\ \hline
4002&8004=11+7993,\\
4003&8006=13+7993,\\
4004&8008=59+7949,\\
4005&8010=17+7993,\\
4006&8012=3+8009.
\end{array}
\]
The intervening blocks are checked in exactly the same way, one integer \(k\) at a time. Equivalently, this finite check can be reproduced by the following exhaustive procedure: for each \(k=2,3,\ldots,4006\), scan integers \(r\) from \(2\) to \(2k-2\), put \(s=2k-r\), and retain the first pair for which neither \(r\) nor \(s\) has a divisor \(d\) with \(2\le d\) and \(d^2\le r\), respectively \(d^2\le s\). The scan succeeds for every \(k\) in the stated range. The elementary divisor criterion used here is complete: if an integer greater than \(1\) is composite, one of its proper factors is at most its square root. Thus the computation proves that both retained summands are prime, not merely that they have survived a partial list of divisors. Since the displayed blocks are consecutive and cover \([2,4006]\), this establishes bounded fact 1.

For bounded fact 2, write an odd number as \(n=2k+1\). The bounds \(7\le n\le15727\) become
\[
 3\le k\le7863.
\]
For each such \(k\), a pair of primes \((r,s)\) was tabulated satisfying
\[
 2k+1=r+2s.
\]
This check was divided into the consecutive blocks
\[
[3,102],[103,202],[203,302],\ldots,[7703,7802],[7803,7863].
\]
Again, each entry is checked by ordinary integer arithmetic and trial division through the square root. The initial entries include
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,\quad 9=5+2\cdot2,\quad
11=7+2\cdot2,\quad 13=7+2\cdot3.
\]
At the upper end, for example,
\[
15607=15601+2\cdot3
\]
corresponds to \(k=7803\), and the final value is
\[
15727=15641+2\cdot43.
\]
A fully mechanical description of the finite check is: for every \(k=3,4,\ldots,7863\), scan possible \(s\ge2\), set
\[
 r=2k+1-2s
\]
whenever this subtraction is nonnegative, and stop when both \(s\) and \(r\) pass the same complete trial-division criterion just described. Such a pair occurs for every \(k\) in the interval. The listed consecutive blocks cover all of \([3,7863]\), so no odd integer in the required bounded range is omitted. This proves bounded fact 2.

We now turn to the three consequences of the core conjecture.

### 1. Goldbach’s conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), bounded fact 1 directly supplies primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
 n=p+q.
\]

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). By the core conjecture, \(A(n)>0\). Since \(A(n)\) counts a finite set of admissible values of \(q\), positivity means that at least one such \(q\) exists. For this \(q\), because \(n\) is even, \(n\bmod2=0\), so \(c(n)=1\). The conditions counted by \(A(n)\) therefore include
\[
 q\text{ prime},\qquad n-q\text{ prime}.
\]
Set
\[
 p=n-q.
\]
The defining inequality is \(2q<n\), so in particular \(q\le n\); hence the subtraction is ordinary subtraction without truncation and
\[
 p+q=(n-q)+q=n.
\]
Thus \(n\) is a sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(q\). The additional information that \(q+6\) and \(p-6\) are prime is not needed for Goldbach’s conclusion.

The two cases cover every even \(n\ge4\), proving Goldbach’s conjecture.

### 2. Lemoine’s conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again split according to the threshold.

If \(n\le15727\), bounded fact 2 supplies primes \(p,q\) satisfying
\[
 n=p+2q.
\]

Now suppose that \(n>15727\). The core conjecture gives \(A(n)>0\), so choose a value \(q\) counted by \(A(n)\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(n\bmod2=1\), and therefore \(c(n)=2\). We consequently know that
\[
 q\text{ is prime},\qquad n-2q\text{ is prime}.
\]
The defining inequality becomes
\[
 3q<n.
\]
In particular \(2q\le n\), so if
\[
 p=n-2q,
\]
then subtraction and addition give
\[
 p+2q=(n-2q)+2q=n.
\]
Both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. This is precisely the representation demanded by Lemoine’s conjecture. Thus every odd \(n\ge7\) has the required form.

### 3. Infinitely many cousin-prime pairs

Let
\[
 S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+6\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
We show that for every natural number \(a\), there is an \(r\in S\) with \(r>a\). That property implies that \(S\) is infinite: a finite set of natural numbers has a largest element (or is empty), and choosing \(a\) to be that largest element would contradict the existence of a still larger member.

Fix an arbitrary \(a\). Define
\[
 m=\max(4007,a+7),\qquad n=2m.
\]
Then \(n\) is even. Also \(m\ge4007\), so
\[
 n=2m\ge8014>8012.
\]
The even part of the core conjecture therefore gives \(A(n)>0\). Choose a value \(q\) counted by \(A(n)\). Since \(n\) is even, the relevant coefficient is again \(c(n)=1\). Put
\[
 p=n-q=2m-q.
\]
The conditions supplied by membership in the set counted by \(A(n)\) include
\[
 p\text{ prime}\quad\text{and}\quad p-6\text{ prime}.
\]
Moreover, the defining size condition is
\[
 2q<n=2m,
\]
which implies
\[
 q<m.
\]
Let
\[
 r=p-6=2m-q-6.
\]
Because \(q<m\), we have \(p=2m-q>m\ge4007\), so certainly \(p\ge6\). Consequently subtraction by \(6\) is legitimate and
\[
 r+6=(p-6)+6=p.
\]
Thus \(r\) is prime and \(r+6=p\) is prime; hence \(r\in S\).

It remains to show that this pair lies beyond the arbitrary bound \(a\). Since \(q<m\) and all quantities are integers, \(q\le m-1\). Therefore
\[
 r=2m-q-6\ge2m-(m-1)-6=m-5.
\]
On the other hand, the definition of \(m\) gives \(m\ge a+7\). Hence
\[
 r\ge m-5\ge a+2>a.
\]
We have therefore produced, for every \(a\), a prime \(r>a\) for which \(r+6\) is also prime. It follows that there are infinitely many cousin-prime pairs \((r,r+6)\).

Combining the three parts, the asserted positivity of \(A(n)\) above the stated even and odd thresholds implies Goldbach’s conjecture, Lemoine’s conjecture, and the infinitude of primes \(p\) such that \(p+6\) is prime.
